reading.rtitle: The First Sentence Is a Door
paras: Every writing teacher has a private collection of first sentences, and most of them are not kept because they are good. 'Webster's Dictionary defines art as' is a classic of the genre. So is 'Ever since I was a child, I have been fascinated by', and its close cousin, 'In today's world'. None of these sentences is wrong. Each is simply a door that opens onto a hallway the reader has walked down many times before, and a reader who has walked it that often will not linger.

Rarely does a first sentence survive the first draft, and there is a good reason for that. When we begin to write, we are still discovering what we want to say, and our opening lines tend to record that search rather than its result. The early paragraphs of a personal essay are often inchoate: they circle the subject, supply background and announce significance before the writer has earned it. Only later, usually in the third or fourth paragraph, does the essay stumble onto a moment that actually resonates. The most useful piece of revision advice I know is also the simplest. Find that moment and move it to the top.

Beginning in medias res, in the middle of the action, is one way of honoring that advice. A student of mine once opened an essay with a museum guard warning her, for the fourth time, to step back from a painting. Nothing about the sentence was dramatic. Nobody was in danger. Yet the reader was immediately inside a small conflict, curious about a girl who kept stepping over a line on a gallery floor, and willing to wait for an explanation. The explanation, when it arrived two paragraphs later, meant far more than it would have in the first line.

The same principle lies behind the most repeated rule in writing classrooms: show, don't tell. A sentence such as 'I was extremely nervous before my portfolio review' reports a feeling and asks the reader to take it on trust. A sentence that describes two damp handprints on the cover of a portfolio produces the feeling instead, and lets the reader reach the conclusion alone. People are more easily persuaded by conclusions they draw themselves, and admissions readers are no exception.

The rule has limits, however, and they are worth reckoning with. An essay that only shows becomes a sequence of vivid vignettes with no mind behind them. At some point the writer must step out of the scene and interrogate it: what did the moment mean, what did it change, what question did it precipitate? Reflection is not a failure to show. It is the part of the essay in which the reader finally meets the writer's thinking, and a tentative, honest reflection is almost always more convincing than a perfect epiphany.

Nor is there a single correct kind of opening. Some of the best essays begin with a paradox, a confession or a question; a few begin, quite calmly, with background, and belie their quiet start with the intensity of what follows. What matters is not the type but the test. The first sentence of a personal statement should be one that only its writer could have written. If a classmate could sign it without changing a word, the door is not yet open.

gist.prompt: Which statement best captures the writer's argument?
choices: Every personal essay must begin in the middle of an action scene.
A strong opening is one only its writer could have written, often found later in the draft and moved to the top.
Reflection weakens personal essays and should be replaced by vivid description.

items: The writer considers dictionary-definition openings grammatically incorrect.
'None of these sentences is wrong.' The problem is that the reader has seen them many times.
According to the writer, the moment that resonates often appears later in an early draft.
'Only later, usually in the third or fourth paragraph, does the essay stumble onto a moment that actually resonates.'
The student's opening about the museum guard was effective because it was highly dramatic.
'Nothing about the sentence was dramatic. Nobody was in danger.' It worked because it created a small conflict.
The writer believes an essay that only shows can lack a thinking mind behind it.
'An essay that only shows becomes a sequence of vivid vignettes with no mind behind them.'
The writer forbids opening a personal statement with background information.
'A few begin, quite calmly, with background.' What matters is the test, not the type.

items.situation: Lift it: "I had never seen a painting so small."
tips: Never had I seen a painting so small.
Negative adverbial first, then auxiliary before subject.

items.situation: Lift it: "I understood what she meant only years later."
tips: Only years later did I understand what she meant.
Only + time expression takes inversion in the main clause.

items.situation: Lift it: "I noticed the signature only when I stepped back."
tips: Not until I stepped back did I notice the signature.
Not until: the inversion comes after the time clause.

items.situation: Lift it: "The room was so dark that I missed the first painting."
tips: So dark was the room that I missed the first painting.
So + adjective + verb + subject, then the result.

items.situation: Show, don't tell: "I was very excited."
tips: I read the acceptance email four times before I let myself scream.
Replace the feeling with a detail that proves it.

items.situation: Fix the costume: "Often did I dream of museums."
tips: Positive adverbs do not invert in modern English. Save inversion for rare, negative or restrictive openings.

listenings.text: Thanks for having me. So, beginnings. When I read manuscripts by people who are just starting out, I notice the same thing almost every time. The first ten pages explain who everyone is, where they live and how they got there. And I understand why. Beginning writers are terrified that the reader will be lost. But a reader who is being given information is not yet a reader who cares. Starting in medias res, in the middle of something that is already happening, fixes that, but it asks something of you as the writer. It asks you to trust the reader. People can live with a little confusion, as long as something is clearly at stake on the page. They will wait for the background if the scene has earned their attention. Now, one warning, because I see this mistake a lot. The action has to matter. If you open with a car chase and the rest of the book is about a quiet marriage, that is not a beginning, it's a trick, and readers notice tricks. The middle you start in has to be the middle of your actual story.

Okay, let's begin with the rule you have all heard a hundred times: show, don't tell. Here's what it actually means. Telling is a sentence like, I was nervous. Showing is a sentence like, my hands left damp prints on the cover of my portfolio. Both sentences give the reader the same information. The difference is who does the work. In the first one, I do the work and you simply believe me. In the second, you look at the detail and you reach the conclusion yourself. And that matters enormously in an application essay, because people believe the conclusions they reach on their own far more than the conclusions they are handed. Now, here's the part that most workshops leave out. The rule has a limit. Not every sentence should show. At some point you have to step out of the scene and tell the reader what it meant, what it changed, what you still don't understand. If you only show, your essay becomes a list of pretty moments, and the reader never meets the person who lived them.
